units.text: INT. FLOODED GRAIN SILO - DAY
Brown water laps at the third rung of the iron ladder.
Light falls in thick shafts through holes in the tin roof.
The walls sweat.
A rotten sweetness hangs in the air, old wheat gone to mold.
MAREN VOSS, forties, a farmer in a soaked canvas jacket, sits on a ledge halfway up the wall, one arm hooked through the ladder, watching the water.

OTIENO, thirties, her neighbor, a mechanic with a split lip, stands waist-deep below, feeling along the wall with both hands, working his way around the curve of the silo until he reaches a bricked-up door, presses his ear to it, and strikes it three times with a bolt while she watches without a word.
Two days. Two days and the river took the whole valley.
units.name: MAREN

units.text: Door's solid. Mortar, not wood.
units.name: OTIENO

units.text: Somebody bricked it up.
units.name: MAREN

units.text: Somebody who didn't want it opened. Or didn't want something in here to get out.
units.name: OTIENO

units.text: She climbs down a rung.
The water touches her boot.
She pulls the boot back up, then plants it again, then looks up at the roof where a pigeon has settled on a strut.
Anybody up there? Anybody hear us?
units.name: MAREN

units.text: Nothing but drip.
Otieno rests his forehead on the bricks.
She wades over to him and presses her palm flat to the wall beside his, and together they listen.
It's quiet.
units.name: OTIENO

units.text: It's never quiet in a silo. There's always the grain settling.
units.name: MAREN

units.text: No grain left to settle.
units.name: OTIENO

units.text: She takes the bolt from his hand and strikes the wall herself, twice, then once, then twice.
A long moment passes.
From beyond the bricks, faint as a heartbeat, someone strikes back.
